The image formed by a concave mirror is observed to be virtual, erect and larger than the object. Where should be the position of the object?
(a) Between the principal focus and the centre of curvature
(b) At the centre of curvature
(c) Beyond the centre of curvature
(d) Between the pole of the mirror and its principal focus.
solution: (d) Between the pole of the mirror and its principal focus. Only in this position does a concave mirror produce a virtual, erect, and magnified (larger) image.
steps: Concave mirror gives virtual, erect, magnified image only when object is between pole and focus
Answer: (d)

question:
Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real image of the size of the object?
(a) At the principal focus of the lens
(b) At twice the focal length
(c) At infinity
(d) Between the optical centre of the lens and its principal focus.
solution: (b) At twice the focal length (2F). When the object is placed at 2F in front of a convex lens, the real image formed is also at 2F on the other side, and is of the same size as the object.
steps: Convex lens: object at 2F gives real image at 2F, same size as object
Answer: (b) at twice the focal length

question:
A spherical mirror and a thin spherical lens have each a focal length of –15 cm. The mirror and the lens are likely to be
(a) both concave.
(b) both convex.
(c) the mirror is concave and the lens is convex.
(d) the mirror is convex, but the lens is concave.
solution: (a) both concave. By the sign convention used, a negative focal length corresponds to a concave mirror (converging) and also to a concave lens (diverging). Since both have f = –15 cm, both the mirror and the lens must be concave.
steps: Negative f: concave mirror has negative f; concave lens also has negative f
Both given f = –15 cm ⇒ both are concave
Answer: (a) both concave

question:
No matter how far you stand from a mirror, your image appears erect. The mirror is likely to be
(a) only plane.
(b) only concave.
(c) only convex.
(d) either plane or convex.
solution: (d) either plane or convex. A plane mirror always forms an erect image (of the same size) at any distance, and a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image at any object distance. A concave mirror, in contrast, gives an erect image only when the object is very close (between pole and focus), and an inverted image otherwise.
steps: Plane mirror: always erect image at any distance
Convex mirror: always virtual, erect image at any distance
Concave mirror does NOT always give erect image — Answer: (d) either plane or convex

question:
Which of the following lenses would you prefer to use while reading small letters found in a dictionary?
(a) A convex lens of focal length 50 cm.
(b) A concave lens of focal length 50 cm.
(c) A convex lens of focal length 5 cm.
(d) A concave lens of focal length 5 cm.
solution: (c) A convex lens of focal length 5 cm. To read small letters, we need a magnifying glass, which must be a convex (converging) lens, and a shorter focal length gives greater magnification when the object is held close to the lens (within its focal length), making tiny print easier to read.
steps: Magnifying glass must be a convex lens (concave lenses can't magnify this way)
Shorter focal length gives greater magnification for close objects
Answer: (c) convex lens of focal length 5 cm

question: We wish to obtain an erect image of an object, using a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. What should be the range of distance of the object from the mirror? What is the nature of the image? Is the image larger or smaller than the object? Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation in this case.
solution:
For a concave mirror to form an erect image, the object must be placed between the pole (P) and the principal focus (F), i.e., at a distance between 0 cm and 15 cm from the mirror (0 < object distance < 15 cm).
In this range, the image formed is virtual, erect, and larger (magnified) than the object, and is formed behind the mirror.
(A ray diagram would show two rays from the object tip — one parallel to the principal axis reflecting through F, and one directed towards the centre of curvature reflecting back on itself — diverging after reflection so that their backward extensions meet behind the mirror to form the enlarged, erect, virtual image.)
steps: Object must lie between pole and focus: 0 cm < distance < 15 cm
In this range, concave mirror gives virtual, erect image
Image is larger (magnified) than the object

question:
Name the type of mirror used in the following situations.
(a) Headlights of a car.
(b) Side/rear-view mirror of a vehicle.
(c) Solar furnace.
Support your answer with reason.
solution:
(a) Headlights of a car — Concave mirror. Placing the bulb at the focus of a concave mirror causes the reflected light rays to travel as a strong, parallel beam over a long distance, giving good illumination.
(b) Side/rear-view mirror — Convex mirror. It always forms an erect (though diminished) image at all object distances and has a wider field of view, letting the driver see a larger area of traffic behind.
(c) Solar furnace — Concave mirror. It converges/concentrates the parallel rays of sunlight falling on it to a single focal point, producing intense heat sufficient to generate high temperatures.
steps: Headlights: concave mirror, converts point source at focus into a parallel beam
Rear-view mirror: convex mirror, always erect image + wide field of view
Solar furnace: concave mirror, concentrates sunlight to focus for maximum heat

question: One-half of a convex lens is covered with a black paper. Will this lens produce a complete image of the object? Verify your answer experimentally. Explain your observations.
solution:
Yes, the lens will still produce a complete image of the object, although the image will be less bright (of lower intensity) than before. This is because every point on the object sends out light rays that spread over the entire surface of the lens; even with half the lens covered, the remaining (uncovered) half still receives and refracts rays coming from every point of the object, so a complete image is formed by that half — just with less total light reaching the image, making it dimmer.
(This can be verified experimentally by covering one half of a convex lens with black paper and using it to form the image of a candle flame on a screen — a complete, though dimmer, image of the flame is seen.)
steps: Every point of the object sends light rays to the whole lens surface
Covering half the lens still leaves rays from all object points reaching the uncovered half
So a complete image still forms, only dimmer (lower intensity)

question: An object 5 cm in length is held 25 cm away from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Draw the ray diagram and find the position, size and the nature of the image formed.
solution:
Given: convex (converging) lens, f = +10 cm, object height h = 5 cm, object distance u = –25 cm.
Using the lens formula 1/v – 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 + 1/(–25) = 1/10 – 1/25 = (5 – 2)/50 = 3/50
v = 50/3 ≈ +16.7 cm.
Magnification, m = v/u = (50/3)/(–25) = –2/3 ≈ –0.67.
Height of image, h′ = m × h = –0.67 × 5 ≈ –3.3 cm.
The image is formed at about 16.7 cm from the lens on the side opposite to the object; it is real, inverted, and diminished (smaller than the object), with a height of about 3.3 cm.
steps: f = +10 cm (convex lens), u = –25 cm; use 1/v – 1/u = 1/f
Solve: v = 50/3 ≈ 16.7 cm
m = v/u ≈ –0.67 ⇒ image is real, inverted, diminished, height ≈ 3.3 cm

question: A concave lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image 10 cm from the lens. How far is the object placed from the lens? Draw the ray diagram.
solution:
Given: concave lens, f = –15 cm. Since a concave lens always forms a virtual image on the same side as the object, image distance v = –10 cm.
Using the lens formula 1/v – 1/u = 1/f:
1/u = 1/v – 1/f = 1/(–10) – 1/(–15) = –1/10 + 1/15 = (–3 + 2)/30 = –1/30
u = –30 cm.
The object is placed 30 cm from the lens (in front of it, on the same side as the virtual image).
steps: Concave lens: f = –15 cm; image is virtual ⇒ v = –10 cm
Use 1/u = 1/v – 1/f
u = –30 cm — object is 30 cm from the lens

question: An object is placed at a distance of 10 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
solution:
Given: convex mirror, f = +15 cm, object distance u = –10 cm.
Using the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/15 – 1/(–10) = 1/15 + 1/10 = (2 + 3)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6
v = +6 cm.
Since v is positive, the image is formed 6 cm behind the mirror; it is virtual and erect.
Magnification, m = –v/u = –6/(–10) = 0.6 (positive and less than 1), so the image is diminished (smaller than the object).
steps: Convex mirror: f = +15 cm, u = –10 cm; use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Solve: v = +6 cm (behind the mirror)
Image is virtual, erect, and diminished (m = 0.6)

question: The magnification produced by a plane mirror is +1. What does this mean?
solution: A magnification of +1 means that the image formed by the plane mirror is of exactly the same size as the object (magnitude of magnification = 1), and the positive sign indicates that the image is virtual and erect (upright, same orientation as the object), as is always the case for a plane mirror.
steps: Magnitude 1 ⇒ image same size as object
Positive sign ⇒ image is virtual and erect
This is always true for a plane mirror

question: An object 5.0 cm in length is placed at a distance of 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm. Find the position of the image, its nature and size.
solution:
Given: convex mirror, R = 30 cm ⇒ f = R/2 = +15 cm. Object height h = 5.0 cm, object distance u = –20 cm.
Using the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/15 – 1/(–20) = 1/15 + 1/20 = (4 + 3)/60 = 7/60
v = 60/7 ≈ +8.6 cm.
Magnification, m = –v/u = –(60/7)/(–20) = 60/140 = 3/7 ≈ 0.43.
Height of image, h′ = m × h ≈ 0.43 × 5.0 ≈ 2.1 cm.
The image is formed about 8.6 cm behind the mirror; it is virtual, erect, and diminished, with a size of about 2.1 cm.
steps: Convex mirror: f = R/2 = +15 cm; u = –20 cm; use mirror formula
Solve: v ≈ +8.6 cm (behind mirror)
m ≈ 0.43 ⇒ image virtual, erect, diminished, size ≈ 2.1 cm

question: An object of size 7.0 cm is placed at 27 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed, so that a sharp focussed image can be obtained? Find the size and the nature of the image.
solution:
Given: concave mirror, f = –18 cm (negative by sign convention), object height h = 7.0 cm, object distance u = –27 cm.
Using the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/(–18) – 1/(–27) = –1/18 + 1/27 = (–3 + 2)/54 = –1/54
v = –54 cm.
So the screen should be placed 54 cm in front of the mirror (since the image is real, it can be captured on a screen there).
Magnification, m = –v/u = –(–54)/(–27) = –2.
Height of image, h′ = m × h = –2 × 7.0 = –14 cm.
The image is real, inverted, and enlarged (magnified 2 times), with a size of 14 cm, formed 54 cm from the mirror.
steps: Concave mirror: f = –18 cm, u = –27 cm; use mirror formula
Solve: v = –54 cm — screen placed 54 cm in front of mirror
m = –2 ⇒ image real, inverted, enlarged, size = 14 cm

question: Find the focal length of a lens of power – 2.0 D. What type of lens is this?
solution:
Power, P = 1/f (f in metres) ⇒ f = 1/P = 1/(–2.0) = –0.5 m = –50 cm.
Since the focal length is negative, this is a concave (diverging) lens.
steps: Negative focal length ⇒ concave (diverging) lens

question: A doctor has prescribed a corrective lens of power +1.5 D. Find the focal length of the lens. Is the prescribed lens diverging or converging?
solution:
Power, P = 1/f (f in metres) ⇒ f = 1/P = 1/1.5 ≈ +0.67 m ≈ +66.7 cm.
Since the focal length (and power) is positive, the lens is a converging (convex) lens.
steps: Positive focal length ⇒ converging (convex) lens

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: What is meant by power of accommodation of the eye?
solution: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length, by the action of the ciliary muscles changing the curvature of the lens, so that the eye can focus on objects at different distances (both near and far), is called the power of accommodation of the eye.
steps: Ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens
This changes the lens's focal length
This lets the eye focus on both near and far objects

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: A person with a myopic eye cannot see objects beyond 1.2 m distinctly. What should be the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision?
solution: A concave (diverging) lens of suitable power should be used. Myopia means the far point of the eye is nearer than infinity (here 1.2 m instead of infinity); a concave lens diverges the incoming parallel rays from a distant object so that their image is formed at the myopic far point (1.2 m) instead of in front of the retina, thus focusing it correctly on the retina.
steps: Myopia = far point closer than infinity (here 1.2 m)
Concave lens diverges light before it enters the eye
This shifts the image back onto the retina

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: What is the far point and near point of the human eye with normal vision?
solution: For a normal human eye, the near point (least distance of distinct vision) is about 25 cm from the eye, and the far point is at infinity.
steps: Near point ≈ 25 cm
Far point = infinity

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: A student has difficulty reading the blackboard while sitting in the last row. What could be the defect the child is suffering from? How can it be corrected?
solution: The child is likely suffering from myopia (near-sightedness) — distant objects (the blackboard) are not seen clearly, while nearby objects can be seen distinctly. This is corrected by using spectacles with a concave (diverging) lens of suitable power, which brings the image of distant objects back onto the retina.
steps: Can't see distant board clearly = myopia
Image of distant objects forms in front of retina
Corrected using a concave lens of suitable power

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to (a) presbyopia. (b) accommodation. (c) near-sightedness. (d) far-sightedness.
solution: Correct option: (b) accommodation. The ability of the eye lens to adjust (change) its focal length so as to focus on objects at varying distances is called accommodation.
steps: Adjusting focal length to focus at different distances = accommodation
Answer: (b)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: The human eye forms the image of an object at its (a) cornea. (b) iris. (c) pupil. (d) retina.
solution: Correct option: (d) retina. The eye lens forms a real, inverted image of the object on the retina, a light-sensitive membrane at the back of the eye; the retina's cells convert this into electrical signals sent to the brain.
steps: Image is formed on the light-sensitive screen at back of eye
That screen is the retina
Answer: (d)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about (a) 25 m. (b) 2.5 cm. (c) 25 cm. (d) 2.5 m.
solution: Correct option: (c) 25 cm. This is the standard near point for a young adult with normal vision.
steps: Near point of normal adult eye = 25 cm
Answer: (c)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the (a) pupil. (b) retina. (c) ciliary muscles. (d) iris.
solution: Correct option: (c) ciliary muscles. Contraction or relaxation of the ciliary muscles changes the curvature of the eye lens, which changes its focal length (this is accommodation).
steps: Ciliary muscles contract/relax
This changes the eye lens's curvature and hence focal length
Answer: (c)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: A person needs a lens of power –5.5 dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power +1.5 dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?
solution:
Focal length f = 1/P (in metres).
(i) Distant vision: P = –5.5 D, so f = 1/(–5.5) = –0.182 m ≈ –18.2 cm. (A concave lens of focal length about 18.2 cm, for correcting myopia.)
(ii) Near vision: P = +1.5 D, so f = 1/1.5 = 0.667 m ≈ 66.7 cm. (A convex lens of focal length about 66.7 cm, for correcting hypermetropia.)
steps: f = 1/P
Distant: f = 1/(-5.5) ≈ -18.2 cm (concave lens)
Near: f = 1/1.5 ≈ 66.7 cm (convex lens)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?
solution:
A concave (diverging) lens is required. For a distant object (u = –∞), the lens must form a virtual image at the person's far point (v = –80 cm = –0.8 m).
Using 1/f = 1/v – 1/u = 1/(–0.8) – 1/(–∞) = –1.25 per m.
So f = –0.8 m, and Power P = 1/f = 1/(–0.8) = –1.25 D.
The lens required is a concave lens of power –1.25 D.
steps: Image of a distant object must form at the far point (80 cm)
f = -0.8 m, P = 1/f = -1.25 D (concave lens)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
solution:
(Diagram: a convex lens placed in front of the hypermetropic eye converges the rays from a nearby object at 25 cm so that they appear to come from the person's near point at 1 m, forming a virtual image there — not reproduced here, only the calculation.)
For an object placed at the normal near point, u = –25 cm = –0.25 m, the lens must form a virtual image at the person's near point, v = –1 m.
1/f = 1/v – 1/u = 1/(–1) – 1/(–0.25) = –1 + 4 = 3 per m.
So f = 1/3 m ≈ 0.33 m, and Power P = 1/f = +3 D.
A convex lens of power +3 dioptres is required.
steps: Object at 25 cm; image must form at near point 1 m (hypermetropia)
P = 1/f = +3 D (convex lens)

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
solution: To see an object clearly, the ciliary muscles must contract enough to increase the curvature (decrease the focal length) of the eye lens so that the image forms exactly on the retina. For objects closer than 25 cm, the required curvature/converging power is greater than the eye lens can achieve — the ciliary muscles cannot contract beyond a certain limit. So the image is not sharply focused on the retina, and such close objects appear blurred, causing eye strain.
steps: Seeing very close objects needs very high converging power of the lens
Ciliary muscles have a maximum limit of contraction/curvature change
Beyond 25 cm closer, the eye can't achieve enough power, image blurs

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
solution: The image distance in the eye does not change — the eye lens always forms the image on the retina, whose distance from the lens is fixed (the eyeball's dimensions do not change). Instead, when the object distance increases, the ciliary muscles relax, decreasing the curvature of the eye lens and increasing its focal length, so that the image still forms exactly on the retina. It is the focal length of the eye lens that changes (accommodation), not the image distance.
steps: Retina position is fixed, so image distance stays the same
Eye lens's focal length changes instead (via ciliary muscles)
This is the process of accommodation

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: Why do stars twinkle?
solution: Starlight undergoes continuous refraction as it passes through the earth's atmosphere, which has continuously and randomly varying refractive index (due to changing temperature/density of air layers). Since stars are very far away, they act as point sources of light. The changing atmospheric refraction causes the apparent position of the star, and the amount of starlight reaching the eye, to fluctuate randomly — the star appears sometimes brighter and sometimes fainter. This flickering effect is the twinkling of stars.
steps: Atmosphere's refractive index keeps fluctuating (turbulence)
Stars are point sources, so their light path bends slightly and randomly
Apparent brightness/position fluctuates → twinkling

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: Explain why the planets do not twinkle.
solution: Planets are much closer to the earth than stars and are seen as extended sources of light (not point sources) — they can be considered a collection of a very large number of point-sized sources of light. The total variation in light received from all these individual point sources averages out to zero, cancelling the twinkling (flickering) effect that would occur from any single point source. Hence planets appear to shine steadily.
steps: Planets are close, so appear as extended sources, not point sources
Extended source = many point sources combined
Individual fluctuations average out to zero → no twinkling

chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
question: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
solution: The blue colour of the sky, as seen from earth, is due to scattering of sunlight by the fine particles/molecules of the atmosphere (finer particles scatter shorter, blue wavelengths more strongly). An astronaut in space (or at very high altitude) is above the earth's atmosphere, or in a region where there is no atmosphere to scatter sunlight. With no scattering of light, there is no blue light being scattered towards the astronaut's eyes, so the sky appears dark (black) instead of blue.
steps: Blue sky is caused by atmospheric scattering of sunlight
Astronaut is above/outside the atmosphere — no scattering medium
No scattering → no blue light reaches the eye → sky looks dark

question: What does an electric circuit mean?
solution: An electric circuit is a continuous and closed path made of a source (cell/battery), connecting wires, and electrical component(s) (such as a switch and a bulb), along which an electric current can flow.
steps: Continuous, closed path
Contains a source, wires, and components
Current flows only when the circuit is closed/complete

question: Define the unit of current.
solution: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A). One ampere is the current that flows when one coulomb of charge flows through a cross-section of a conductor in one second, i.e., 1 A = 1 C/1 s.
steps: Current I = Q/t
1 A = 1 coulomb of charge flowing per second

question: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
solution:
Charge on one electron, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Number of electrons n = Q/e = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
steps: n = Q/e
n = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons

question: Name a device that helps to maintain a potential difference across a conductor.
solution: A cell or a battery (a combination of cells) helps to maintain a potential difference across a conductor.
steps: Chemical action in a cell/battery maintains the potential difference

question: What is meant by saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V?
solution: The potential difference between two points in a current-carrying conductor is 1 V if 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other.
steps: V = W/Q
1 V means 1 J of work moves 1 C of charge between the two points

question: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
solution: Energy given per coulomb = potential difference = V = W/Q, so W = VQ = 6 V × 1 C = 6 J. Each coulomb of charge passing through the battery is given 6 joules of energy.
steps: W = VQ
W = 6 V × 1 C = 6 J

question: On what factors does the resistance of a conductor depend?
solution: The resistance of a conductor depends on: (i) its length (directly proportional, R ∝ l), (ii) its area of cross-section (inversely proportional, R ∝ 1/A), (iii) the nature (material/resistivity) of the conductor, and (iv) its temperature.
steps: R ∝ length (l)
R ∝ 1/area of cross-section (A)
Depends on material (resistivity ρ) and temperature

question: Will current flow more easily through a thick wire or a thin wire of the same material, when connected to the same source? Why?
solution: Current flows more easily through a thick wire. Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section (R = ρl/A); a thick wire has a larger cross-sectional area and hence lower resistance, so for the same potential difference, a larger current flows through it (I = V/R).
steps: R ∝ 1/A
Thick wire → larger A → smaller R
Smaller R → larger current for the same V

question: Let the resistance of an electrical component remains constant while the potential difference across the two ends of the component decreases to half of its former value. What change will occur in the current through it?
solution: By Ohm's law, I = V/R. Since R is constant and V becomes half, the current I also becomes half of its former value.
steps: I = V/R, R constant
V halved ⇒ I halved (Ohm's law)

question: Why are coils of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
solution: Alloys generally have higher resistivity than their constituent pure metals, and importantly they do not oxidise (burn) readily even at high temperatures. This makes alloys (like nichrome) more suitable and durable for use in electrical heating devices such as toasters and electric irons.
steps: Alloys have higher resistivity (more heating effect)
Alloys resist oxidation/burning at high temperature
So alloys are more durable for heating elements

question: Use the data in Table 11.2 to answer the following - (a) Which among iron and mercury is a better conductor? (b) Which material is the best conductor?
solution:
(a) Iron (resistivity 10.0 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) has lower resistivity than mercury (94.0 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m), so iron is a better conductor than mercury.
(b) Silver has the lowest resistivity (1.60 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) among the substances listed, so silver is the best conductor.
steps: Lower resistivity = better conductor
Iron (10×10⁻⁸) < Mercury (94×10⁻⁸) → iron is better conductor
Silver has the lowest resistivity of all → best conductor

question: Draw a schematic diagram of a circuit consisting of a battery of three cells of 2 V each, a 5 Ω resistor, an 8 Ω resistor, and a 12 Ω resistor, and a plug key, all connected in series.
solution: A valid circuit: connect the battery (three 2 V cells in series, giving 6 V total), the 5 Ω, 8 Ω and 12 Ω resistors, and the plug key, all one after another in a single loop (in series), so that the same current flows through every component. (Schematic figure not reproduced here — see Q2 for the readings this circuit would give.)
steps: Battery = 3 × 2 V cells in series = 6 V
All three resistors (5 Ω, 8 Ω, 12 Ω) and the key joined end-to-end in one loop

question: Redraw the circuit of Question 1, putting in an ammeter to measure the current through the resistors and a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across the 12 Ω resistor. What would be the readings in the ammeter and the voltmeter?
solution:
Total resistance (series) Rs = 5 + 8 + 12 = 25 Ω.
Total EMF, V = 3 × 2 V = 6 V.
Current, I = V/Rs = 6/25 = 0.24 A. (The ammeter, wherever placed in the series loop, reads 0.24 A.)
Potential difference across the 12 Ω resistor: V₁₂ = I × R = 0.24 A × 12 Ω = 2.88 V. (This is the voltmeter reading.)
steps: I = V/Rs = 6/25 = 0.24 A (ammeter reading)
V across 12 Ω = I×R = 0.24×12 = 2.88 V (voltmeter reading)

question: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel - (a) 1 Ω and 10⁶ Ω, (b) 1 Ω and 10³ Ω, and 10⁶ Ω.
solution:
(a) 1/R = 1/1 + 1/10⁶ = 1.000001, so R ≈ 0.999999 Ω ≈ 1 Ω. The equivalent resistance is very close to, and always slightly less than, the smallest individual resistance (1 Ω).
(b) 1/R = 1/1 + 1/10³ + 1/10⁶ = 1 + 0.001 + 0.000001 = 1.001001, so R ≈ 0.999 Ω ≈ 1 Ω. Again, the equivalent resistance is dominated by, and slightly less than, the smallest resistance (1 Ω).
steps: In parallel, 1/R = sum of 1/Ri
A very large resistance contributes almost nothing to 1/R
Equivalent resistance ends up just under the smallest resistor's value (≈1 Ω in both cases)

question: An electric lamp of 100 Ω, a toaster of resistance 50 Ω, and a water filter of resistance 500 Ω are connected in parallel to a 220 V source. What is the resistance of an electric iron connected to the same source that takes as much current as all three appliances, and what is the current through it?
solution:
Current through lamp, I₁ = 220/100 = 2.2 A
Current through toaster, I₂ = 220/50 = 4.4 A
Current through water filter, I₃ = 220/500 = 0.44 A
Total current of the three appliances, I = I₁+I₂+I₃ = 2.2+4.4+0.44 = 7.04 A
The electric iron must draw the same current, 7.04 A, at 220 V.
Resistance of the iron, R = V/I = 220/7.04 ≈ 31.25 Ω.
Current through the iron = 7.04 A.
steps: Find each appliance's current: I=V/R
Sum currents: I = 2.2+4.4+0.44 = 7.04 A
Iron resistance R = 220/7.04 ≈ 31.25 Ω, current = 7.04 A

question: What are the advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel with the battery instead of connecting them in series?
solution: In a parallel connection: (i) each device gets the full source voltage, regardless of the other devices, so each works at its rated voltage; (ii) devices with different power/current ratings can operate correctly together (unlike in series, where the same current flows through all, which is impractical); (iii) each device can be switched on/off independently without affecting the others; (iv) if one device fails or is switched off, the rest keep working (the circuit is not broken), unlike in series where one failure breaks the whole circuit.
steps: Each device gets full voltage and can have its own switch
Devices with different current needs can all work properly
If one device fails, others keep working (unlike in series)

question: How can three resistors of resistances 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω be connected to give a total resistance of (a) 4 Ω, (b) 1 Ω?
solution:
(a) Connect the 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors in parallel, and connect this combination in series with the 2 Ω resistor.
Parallel of 3 Ω and 6 Ω: 1/R = 1/3+1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.
Total (in series with 2 Ω) = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. ✓
(b) Connect all three resistors (2 Ω, 3 Ω, 6 Ω) in parallel.
1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6+2/6+1/6 = 6/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω. ✓
steps: (a) (3Ω ∥ 6Ω) = 2Ω, then + 2Ω in series = 4Ω

question: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 Ω, 8 Ω, 12 Ω, 24 Ω?
solution:
(a) Highest resistance is obtained by connecting all four in series: R = 4+8+12+24 = 48 Ω.
(b) Lowest resistance is obtained by connecting all four in parallel: 1/R = 1/4+1/8+1/12+1/24 = 6/24+3/24+2/24+1/24 = 12/24 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.
steps: Highest = all in series: 4+8+12+24 = 48 Ω
Lowest = all in parallel: 1/R = 1/4+1/8+1/12+1/24 = 1/2 → R = 2 Ω

question: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?
solution: The cord is made of copper (a good conductor with very low resistance), while the heating element is made of a high-resistance alloy such as nichrome. Since heat produced H = I²Rt, for the same current, the heating element (high R) develops much more heat and gets hot enough to glow, whereas the connecting cord (very low R) develops negligible heat and stays cool, so it does not glow.
steps: Cord = copper (very low resistance)
Heating element = alloy (high resistance, e.g. nichrome)
H = I²Rt, same current → far more heat in high-R element → it glows, cord doesn't

question: Compute the heat generated while transferring 96000 coulomb of charge in one hour through a potential difference of 50 V.
solution:
Given Q = 96000 C, V = 50 V.
Heat generated, H = VQ = 50 × 96000 = 4,800,000 J = 4.8 × 10⁶ J.
steps: H = VQ (work done = heat generated)

question: An electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 s.
steps: H = I²Rt

question: What determines the rate at which energy is delivered by a current?
solution: The rate at which energy is delivered by a current is the electric power, P = VI (also written as P = I²R = V²/R), which is determined by the potential difference (V) across, and the current (I) through, the circuit element (equivalently, by the current and the resistance).
steps: Rate of energy delivery = power, P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Determined by potential difference and current (or current and resistance)

question: An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V line. Determine the power of the motor and the energy consumed in 2 h.
solution:
Given I = 5 A, V = 220 V, t = 2 h.
Power, P = VI = 220 × 5 = 1100 W = 1.1 kW.
Energy consumed in 2 h = P × t = 1.1 kW × 2 h = 2.2 kWh (= 2.2 × 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 7.92 × 10⁶ J).
steps: Energy = P×t = 1100 W × 2 h = 2200 Wh = 2.2 kWh

question: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is R', then the ratio R/R' is - (a) 1/25 (b) 1/5 (c) 5 (d) 25
solution:
Each of the 5 equal parts has resistance R/5. For n equal resistors r in parallel, equivalent resistance = r/n.
So R' = (R/5)/5 = R/25.
Therefore R/R' = R/(R/25) = 25.
Correct option: (d) 25.
steps: Each part = R/5
5 equal parts in parallel: R' = (R/5)/5 = R/25
R/R' = 25 → answer (d)

question: Which of the following terms does not represent electrical power in a circuit? (a) I²R (b) IR² (c) VI (d) V²/R
solution:
Electric power P = VI = I²R = V²/R (using V = IR). The term IR² does not equal any of these — it is dimensionally and algebraically incorrect for power.
Correct option: (b) IR².
steps: Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R (all equivalent via Ohm's law)
IR² is not one of these valid forms
Answer: (b)

question: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, the power consumed will be - (a) 100 W (b) 75 W (c) 50 W (d) 25 W
solution:
Resistance of the bulb (constant), R = V²/P = (220)²/100 = 484 Ω.
At 110 V, power consumed = V²/R = (110)²/484 = 12100/484 = 25 W.
Correct option: (d) 25 W.
steps: R = V²/P = 220²/100 = 484 Ω (fixed)
Answer: (d)

question: Two conducting wires of the same material and of equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. The ratio of heat produced in series and parallel combinations would be - (a) 1:2 (b) 2:1 (c) 1:4 (d) 4:1
solution:
Let each wire have resistance r. 
Series: total resistance = 2r, power dissipated = V²/(2r).
Parallel: total resistance = r/2, power dissipated = V²/(r/2) = 2V²/r.
Ratio (series : parallel) = [V²/2r] : [2V²/r] = (1/2) : 2 = 1 : 4.
Correct option: (c) 1:4.
steps: Series R = 2r, power = V²/2r
Parallel R = r/2, power = 2V²/r
Ratio = (1/2r):(2/r) = 1:4 → answer (c)

question: How is a voltmeter connected in the circuit to measure the potential difference between two points?
solution: A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across (between) the two points between which the potential difference is to be measured.
steps: Voltmeter connected in parallel across the component/two points

question: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance 10 Ω? How much does the resistance change if the diameter is doubled?
solution:
Diameter d = 0.5 mm = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m, so area A = πd²/4 = π(5×10⁻⁴)²/4 = 1.9635 × 10⁻⁷ m².
Using R = ρl/A, length l = RA/ρ = (10 × 1.9635×10⁻⁷)/(1.6×10⁻⁸) ≈ 122.7 m.
If the diameter is doubled, area becomes 4 times (A' = 4A), so for the same length, new resistance R' = ρl/A' = R/4 = 10/4 = 2.5 Ω.
So the resistance becomes one-fourth of the original value (drops from 10 Ω to 2.5 Ω, i.e., decreases by 7.5 Ω).
steps: Doubling diameter → A×4 → R becomes R/4 = 2.5 Ω

question: The values of current I flowing in a given resistor for the corresponding values of potential difference V across the resistor are given below - I (amperes): 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; V (volts): 1.6, 3.4, 6.7, 10.2, 13.2. Plot a graph between V and I and calculate the resistance of that resistor.
solution:
The V–I graph is a straight line passing (approximately) through the origin, confirming Ohm's law; its slope gives the resistance.
R = V/I for each pair: 1.6/0.5=3.2, 3.4/1.0=3.4, 6.7/2.0=3.35, 10.2/3.0=3.4, 13.2/4.0=3.3 (all ohms).
Average value ≈ 3.3–3.4 Ω. So the resistance of the resistor is about 3.3 Ω (taking the slope of the best-fit straight line through these points).
steps: Ohm's law: V/I should be constant = R
Compute V/I for each pair — all close to ~3.3-3.4 Ω
Resistance ≈ 3.3 Ω (slope of straight-line graph)

question: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor.
steps: R = V/I

question: A battery of 9 V is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 Ω, 0.3 Ω, 0.4 Ω, 0.5 Ω and 12 Ω, respectively. How much current would flow through the 12 Ω resistor?
solution:
Total resistance (series) = 0.2+0.3+0.4+0.5+12 = 13.4 Ω.
Current, I = V/R = 9/13.4 ≈ 0.67 A.
Since it's a series circuit, the same current (≈0.67 A) flows through the 12 Ω resistor (and every other resistor).
steps: Series circuit: same current through every resistor, including 12 Ω

question: How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
solution:
Required total resistance, R = V/I = 220/5 = 44 Ω.
For n identical 176 Ω resistors in parallel: R = 176/n, so n = 176/44 = 4.
Four 176 Ω resistors in parallel are required.
steps: Total R needed = V/I = 220/5 = 44 Ω
n resistors of 176 Ω in parallel: R = 176/n

question: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 6 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 9 Ω, (ii) 4 Ω.
solution:
(i) 9 Ω: Connect two of the 6 Ω resistors in parallel (giving 6∥6 = 3 Ω), and connect this combination in series with the third 6 Ω resistor: 3 + 6 = 9 Ω.
(ii) 4 Ω: Connect two of the 6 Ω resistors in series (giving 6+6 = 12 Ω), and connect this combination in parallel with the third 6 Ω resistor: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/12+2/12 = 3/12, so R = 4 Ω.
steps: (i) (6Ω∥6Ω)=3Ω, then +6Ω in series = 9Ω

question: Several electric bulbs designed to be used on a 220 V electric supply line, are rated 10 W. How many lamps can be connected in parallel with each other across the two wires of 220 V line if the maximum allowable current is 5 A?
solution:
Current drawn by each bulb, i = P/V = 10/220 A.
Number of bulbs, n = total allowable current / current per bulb = 5 / (10/220) = 5 × 220/10 = 110.
So 110 bulbs can be connected in parallel.
steps: Current per bulb = P/V = 10/220 A
n = 110 bulbs

question: A hot plate of an electric oven connected to a 220 V line has two resistance coils A and B, each of 24 Ω resistance, which may be used separately, in series, or in parallel. What are the currents in the three cases?
solution:
Separately (using one coil alone): R = 24 Ω, I = V/R = 220/24 ≈ 9.17 A.
Series (A and B together): R = 24+24 = 48 Ω, I = 220/48 ≈ 4.58 A.
Parallel (A and B together): 1/R = 1/24+1/24 = 2/24, R = 12 Ω, I = 220/12 ≈ 18.33 A.
steps: Separate: R=24Ω, I=220/24≈9.17A
Parallel: R=12Ω, I=220/12≈18.33A

question: Compare the power used in the 2 Ω resistor in each of the following circuits: (i) a 6 V battery in series with 1 Ω and 2 Ω resistors, and (ii) a 4 V battery in parallel with 12 Ω and 2 Ω resistors.
solution:
(i) Series circuit: Total R = 1+2 = 3 Ω. Current I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A (same current flows through the 2 Ω resistor). Power in 2 Ω resistor, P = I²R = (2)²×2 = 8 W.
(ii) Parallel circuit: The 2 Ω resistor gets the full battery voltage, 4 V (since it's directly across the battery, in parallel with the 12 Ω resistor). Power in 2 Ω resistor, P = V²/R = (4)²/2 = 8 W.
Both circuits dissipate the same power, 8 W, in the 2 Ω resistor — the ratio is 1:1.
steps: (i) Series: I=6/3=2A; P=I²R=2²×2=8W
(ii) Parallel: full 4V across 2Ω; P=V²/R=4²/2=8W
Both give 8 W — ratio 1:1

question: Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V, and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to electric mains supply. What current is drawn from the line if the supply voltage is 220 V?
solution:
Current through 100 W lamp, I₁ = P/V = 100/220 ≈ 0.4545 A.
Current through 60 W lamp, I₂ = 60/220 ≈ 0.2727 A.
Since in parallel, total current from the line = I₁+I₂ ≈ 0.4545+0.2727 = 0.727 A ≈ 0.73 A.
steps: Total (parallel) I = I1+I2 ≈ 0.73 A

question: Which uses more energy, a 250 W TV set in 1 hr, or a 1200 W toaster in 10 minutes?
solution:
Energy used by TV = P×t = 250 W × 1 h = 250 Wh = 0.25 kWh.
Energy used by toaster = 1200 W × (10/60) h = 1200 × 0.1667 = 200 Wh = 0.2 kWh.
Since 0.25 kWh > 0.2 kWh, the TV set uses more energy than the toaster in this case.
steps: Toaster: 1200 W × (1/6) h = 200 Wh = 0.2 kWh
TV (0.25 kWh) uses more energy than toaster (0.2 kWh)

question: An electric heater of resistance 44 Ω draws 5 A from the service mains for 2 hours. Calculate the rate at which heat is developed in the heater.
solution:
Rate of heat development = power, P = I²R = (5)² × 44 = 25 × 44 = 1100 W (i.e., 1100 J/s).
(Total heat developed in 2 hours = P×t = 1100 W × 7200 s = 7.92 × 10⁶ J.)
steps: Rate of heat = Power = I²R

question: Explain the following. (a) Why is the tungsten used almost exclusively for filament of electric lamps? (b) Why are the conductors of electric heating devices, such as bread-toasters and electric irons, made of an alloy rather than a pure metal? (c) Why is the series arrangement not used for domestic circuits? (d) How does the resistance of a wire vary with its area of cross-section? (e) Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission?
solution:
(a) Tungsten has a very high melting point (about 3380°C) and can be heated to high temperatures (to emit bright light) without melting; it also retains heat well, making it ideal for lamp filaments.
(b) Alloys have higher resistivity than pure metals (so they heat up more for the same current) and, importantly, they do not oxidise (burn) easily even at high operating temperatures, making them more durable for heating elements.
(c) In a series circuit, the same current flows through all appliances, but different appliances need different operating currents; also, if one component fails or is switched off, the entire circuit breaks and all other appliances stop working. Hence domestic circuits use parallel connections instead.
(d) Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section (R ∝ 1/A) — resistance decreases as the cross-sectional area increases.
(e) Copper and aluminium have low resistivity (they are good conductors), so they cause little energy loss (heating) during transmission over long distances; they are also relatively abundant/inexpensive and mechanically workable into wires.
steps: (a) High melting point of tungsten prevents it melting when hot/glowing
(b) Alloys resist oxidation and have higher resistivity, more durable for heating
(c) Series: same current everywhere + one failure breaks all — unsuitable for domestic use
(e) Copper/aluminium have low resistivity → less transmission loss

question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
solution: A compass needle is itself a small bar magnet, free to rotate. When brought near a bar magnet, it experiences the magnetic field (force) of the bar magnet — its north pole is attracted/repelled by the poles of the bar magnet (unlike poles attract, like poles repel) — so the needle turns and aligns itself along the direction of the magnetic field of the bar magnet at that point, causing the observed deflection.
steps: Compass needle is itself a tiny magnet
It experiences the bar magnet's magnetic field (force)
It aligns along the field direction at that point → deflects

question: List the properties of magnetic field lines.
solution:
(i) Magnetic field lines are closed curves — they emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole outside the magnet, and travel from south pole to north pole inside the magnet.
(ii) The direction of the field at any point is given by the tangent to the field line at that point (this is the direction a compass north pole would point).
(iii) The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines — crowded lines indicate a stronger field, and lines farther apart indicate a weaker field.
(iv) No two field lines ever cross/intersect each other.
steps: Closed curves: N pole to S pole outside, S to N inside the magnet
Tangent at a point gives field direction there
Crowding of lines shows field strength; lines never intersect

question: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
solution: If two field lines were to intersect, then at the point of intersection there would be two different directions of the magnetic field (one along each line) at the same point. Since a compass needle placed there can only point in one direction, and the magnetic field at a given point can only have one unique direction, this is impossible. Hence, magnetic field lines never cross each other.
steps: A field line's direction = the field's direction at that point
At an intersection, two directions would be implied for one point
A magnetic field can only have one direction at a point — so lines can't cross

question: Consider a circular loop of wire lying in the plane of the table. Let the current pass through the loop clockwise. Apply the right-hand rule to find out the direction of the magnetic field inside and outside the loop.
solution: Curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current (clockwise, as seen from above the table); the thumb then points in the direction of the field inside the loop. For a clockwise current (viewed from above), the thumb points downward, into the table. So the magnetic field inside the loop points vertically downward (into the table), and outside the loop the field lines curve around and point upward (emerging on the outside and curling back), consistent with the field lines forming closed loops (similar to a bar magnet's field, with the loop's lower face acting like a north pole and the upper face like a south pole in this case).
steps: Curl right-hand fingers in current's direction (clockwise from above)
Thumb (field direction) points downward through the loop
Inside the loop, field points down (into table); outside, field lines curve back around and point up

question: Choose the correct option. The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid-carrying current (a) is zero. (b) decreases as we move towards its end. (c) increases as we move towards its end. (d) is the same at all points.
solution: Correct option: (d) is the same at all points. Inside a long solenoid, the field lines run as parallel straight lines, meaning the magnetic field is uniform (same magnitude and direction) at all points well inside the solenoid.
steps: Field lines inside a long solenoid are straight and parallel
Parallel field lines = uniform field
Answer: (d)

question: Which of the following property of a proton can change while it moves freely in a magnetic field? (There may be more than one correct answer.) (a) mass (b) speed (c) velocity (d) momentum
solution:
Correct options: (c) velocity and (d) momentum.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it does no work on the charge — hence it cannot change the charge's speed (kinetic energy), and mass is unaffected too. However, since the force continually changes the direction of motion, both the velocity (a vector, whose direction changes) and the momentum (mass × velocity, also a vector) change, even though their magnitudes (speed, and magnitude of momentum) remain constant.
steps: Magnetic force is always ⟂ to velocity → does no work → speed (and mass) unchanged
But direction of motion keeps changing
So velocity and momentum (vectors) change — answers (c) and (d)

question: In Activity 12.7, how do we think the displacement of rod AB will be affected if (i) current in rod AB is increased; (ii) a stronger horse-shoe magnet is used; and (iii) length of the rod AB is increased?
solution:
The force (and hence the displacement) on the current-carrying rod depends on the current, the magnetic field strength, and the length of the rod in the field.
(i) If the current in rod AB is increased, the force on it increases, so the displacement increases.
(ii) If a stronger magnet is used (stronger magnetic field), the force increases, so the displacement increases.
(iii) If the length of rod AB (within the field) is increased, the force on it increases, so the displacement increases.
In all three cases, the displacement of the rod increases.
steps: Force on rod ∝ current × field strength × length (F = BIL)
Increasing any one of I, B, or L increases the force
So displacement increases in all three cases

question: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is (a) towards south (b) towards east (c) downward (d) upward
solution:
Using the Lorentz force relation F = qv × B (or Fleming's left-hand rule, since the alpha-particle is positively charged, its motion direction is the same as conventional current direction): with velocity (current) towards west and the resulting force towards north, working out the vector directions shows the magnetic field must point vertically upward.
Correct option: (d) upward.
steps: Positive charge: current direction = velocity direction = west
Force (deflection) is towards north
Applying F = qv×B / Fleming's left-hand rule gives B pointing upward — answer (d)

question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
solution:
(i) Use of an electric fuse (or MCB) in the circuit, which melts/trips and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds a safe limit (due to short-circuiting or overloading), protecting the circuit and appliances.
(ii) Earthing of the metallic bodies of appliances, using a three-pin plug connected to an earth wire, which provides a safe, low-resistance path for any leakage current to the ground, preventing severe electric shocks to the user.
steps: Electric fuse/MCB: breaks circuit on overcurrent (short circuit/overload)
Earthing: connects metallic body to earth, safely diverts leakage current

question: An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic electric circuit (220 V) that has a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? Explain.
solution:
Current drawn by the oven, I = P/V = 2000 W/220 V ≈ 9.09 A.
This exceeds the circuit's rated current capacity of 5 A. As a result, the circuit would be overloaded — the current flowing would be more than the circuit (and its fuse) is designed to carry safely. This would cause the fuse in the circuit to blow (melt) and break the circuit, protecting it from damage; if there were no fuse, the excess current could overheat the wiring and cause a fire hazard. This oven should therefore be connected to a higher-current-rated circuit (e.g., the 15 A circuit), not the 5 A one.
steps: Current drawn = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.09 A
This exceeds the circuit's 5 A rating → overload
Fuse blows / risk of overheating — oven needs a higher-rated (15 A) circuit

question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
solution: To avoid overloading: use separate circuits (with appropriately rated fuses) for high-power appliances (like geysers, air conditioners, heaters) and low-power appliances (like bulbs, fans); avoid connecting too many appliances to a single socket/circuit at the same time; do not exceed the current rating of a circuit; use appropriately rated fuses/MCBs; and ensure proper earthing of appliances and avoid faulty/damaged wiring that could cause short-circuits.
steps: Use separate circuits for high-power vs low-power appliances
Don't overload a single socket/circuit with too many devices
Use correctly rated fuses/MCBs and maintain proper wiring/earthing

question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire? (a) The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire. (b) The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire. (c) The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire. (d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
solution: Correct option: (d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire. The magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire form concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire, centred on the wire, with the field getting weaker (circles more widely spaced) farther from the wire.
steps: Field lines around a straight wire = concentric circles centred on the wire
Answer: (d)

question: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit (a) reduces substantially. (b) does not change. (c) increases heavily. (d) vary continuously.
solution: Correct option: (c) increases heavily. In a short circuit, the live and neutral wires touch directly, drastically reducing the resistance of the circuit, so (by Ohm's law, I=V/R) the current increases abruptly and heavily.
steps: Short circuit = live and neutral wires touch → resistance drops sharply
I = V/R → current rises abruptly
Answer: (c)

question: State whether the following statements are true or false. (a) The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines. (b) A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
solution:
(a) True. Inside a long current-carrying coil (solenoid), the magnetic field lines run as parallel straight lines, giving a uniform field, including at the centre.
(b) False. A wire with green insulation is usually the earth wire, not the live wire. The live wire has red insulation, and the neutral wire has black insulation.
steps: (a) True — field inside a long coil/solenoid is uniform, parallel straight lines
(b) False — green wire is the earth wire; live wire is red

question: List two methods of producing magnetic fields.
solution:
(i) By passing an electric current through a conductor (e.g., a straight wire, a circular loop/coil, or a solenoid) — this produces a magnetic field around it.
(ii) By using a permanent magnet (e.g., a bar magnet), which has a magnetic field around it due to the magnetic properties of its material.
steps: Passing current through a conductor (wire/coil/solenoid)
Using a permanent (bar) magnet

question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
solution: The force is largest when the direction of the current in the conductor is at right angles (perpendicular, 90°) to the direction of the magnetic field.
steps: Force on conductor is maximum when current direction ⟂ magnetic field direction

question: Imagine that you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of magnetic field?
solution: The electron (negative charge) moves forward (toward the front wall), so the conventional current direction is backward (toward the back wall, since current direction is opposite to electron motion). The force on it deflects the beam to your right. Applying the motional force relation F = qv × B (equivalently, Fleming's left-hand rule with current taken opposite to the electron's motion) shows that the magnetic field must be directed vertically downward for this to happen.
steps: Electron moves forward; conventional current is backward (opposite to electron flow)
Deflection (force) is to the observer's right
Using F = qv×B (or Fleming's left-hand rule with reversed current) gives B pointing vertically downward

question: State the rule to determine the direction of a (i) magnetic field produced around a straight conductor-carrying current, (ii) force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field which is perpendicular to it, and (iii) current induced in a coil due to its rotation in a magnetic field.
solution:
(i) Right-hand thumb rule (Maxwell's corkscrew rule): if the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of current flow in the straight conductor, the direction in which the fingers curl gives the direction of the magnetic field lines around it.
(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, the thumb gives the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor.
(iii) Fleming's right-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the thumb in the direction of motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current.
steps: (i) Right-hand thumb rule → field direction around a current-carrying wire
(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule → force on a current-carrying conductor in a field
(iii) Fleming's right-hand rule → induced current direction in a rotating coil

question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
solution: An electric short circuit occurs when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact with each other (for example, due to damaged/worn insulation of the wires or a fault in an appliance), causing the circuit's resistance to drop sharply and the current to increase abruptly to a very high (unsafe) value.
steps: Live wire touches neutral wire directly (insulation damage/fault)
Resistance drops sharply, current rises abruptly to unsafe levels

question: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
solution: The earth wire (usually with green insulation) connects the metallic body of an electrical appliance to a metal plate buried deep in the earth, providing a low-resistance conducting path to the ground. It is necessary to earth metallic appliances so that if there is any leakage of current to the metallic body (due to a fault), the current is safely conducted away into the earth, keeping the appliance's body at (near) earth potential — this prevents the user from experiencing a severe electric shock upon touching the appliance.
steps: Earth wire connects appliance's metal body to the ground (low-resistance path)
Any leaked current flows safely to earth instead of through the user
This prevents severe electric shocks from faulty metallic appliances

question: What are trophic levels? Give an example of a food chain and state the different trophic levels in it.
solution:
Each step or level in a food chain, at which organisms feed on the level below it, is called a trophic level.
Example food chain: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle.
Trophic level 1: Grass (producer/autotroph, makes its own food).
Trophic level 2: Grasshopper (primary consumer/herbivore, eats grass).
Trophic level 3: Frog (secondary consumer, eats the grasshopper).
Trophic level 4: Snake (tertiary consumer, eats the frog).
Trophic level 5: Eagle (quaternary consumer/top predator, eats the snake).
steps: Trophic level = a feeding step/level in a food chain
Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle
Grass=producer(1st); Grasshopper=herbivore(2nd); Frog(3rd); Snake(4th); Eagle(5th, top predator)

question: What is the role of decomposers in the ecosystem?
solution: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the complex organic substances present in the dead remains of plants and animals, and their waste products, into simple inorganic substances. These simple substances go back into the soil (or water) and are reused by plants (producers), recycling nutrients through the ecosystem. In this way, decomposers help maintain the balance of the ecosystem and prevent accumulation of dead matter/waste.
steps: Break down dead organisms and waste into simple inorganic substances
Return nutrients (minerals) to the soil for reuse by producers/plants
Recycle matter and maintain ecosystem balance

question: Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable?
solution: Substances that can be broken down into simpler, harmless substances by biological processes (the action of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms/decomposers) are biodegradable — the enzymes of these decomposers are able to act on their (mostly natural, organic) chemical structure. Substances such as plastics have a chemical structure that natural enzymes/microorganisms cannot break down (enzymes are highly specific in their action), so these substances persist in the environment for a very long time and are called non-biodegradable.
steps: Biodegradable substances can be broken down by microbial/enzymatic action
Non-biodegradable substances (e.g., plastics) have structures that natural enzymes/microbes cannot act on
Enzymes are specific — they can't act on every kind of chemical structure

question: Give any two ways in which biodegradable substances would affect the environment.
solution:
(i) If allowed to accumulate in large quantities before decomposing, biodegradable waste can cause pollution (foul smell, breeding ground for disease-causing organisms/pests) for a period of time.
(ii) On decomposing, they release nutrients back into the soil, enriching it; however, their decomposition (especially in landfills, in the absence of oxygen) can also release gases such as methane, which contributes to environmental/greenhouse gas problems if not managed properly.
steps: Can cause temporary pollution/bad odour/disease spread before decomposing
Decomposition returns nutrients to soil but can also release gases like methane

question: Give any two ways in which non-biodegradable substances would affect the environment.
solution:
(i) They persist in the environment for a very long time without breaking down, accumulating in soil, water bodies, and landfills, and causing long-term pollution (e.g., clogging drains, harming soil fertility).
(ii) They can enter and move through food chains, and if toxic, undergo biological magnification, accumulating in progressively higher concentrations at higher trophic levels and harming organisms (including humans); non-biodegradable litter (like plastics) can also physically harm/kill animals that ingest it.
steps: Persist indefinitely, accumulate and pollute soil/water/land
Can enter food chains, cause biological magnification, and physically harm wildlife

question: What is ozone and how does it affect any ecosystem?
solution: Ozone (O3) is a molecule made up of three atoms of oxygen, present mainly in the upper layers of the atmosphere. There it performs an essential protective function: it shields the earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. Without adequate ozone in the upper atmosphere, more UV radiation would reach the earth's surface, which can damage organisms in an ecosystem — for example, causing skin cancer and other harm in humans and affecting other living organisms too.
steps: Ozone (O3) = molecule of three oxygen atoms, found in upper atmosphere
It absorbs/blocks harmful UV radiation from the sun
Its depletion lets more UV reach earth, damaging organisms (e.g., skin cancer)

question: How can you help in reducing the problem of waste disposal? Give any two methods.
solution:
(i) Segregate waste at source into biodegradable and non-biodegradable categories, and reduce, reuse and recycle non-biodegradable materials (like plastic, paper, glass, metal) instead of discarding them.
(ii) Convert biodegradable kitchen/garden waste into compost or vermicompost (for use as manure) instead of throwing it away, and reduce the use of non-biodegradable items (e.g., use cloth bags instead of plastic bags) to reduce the amount of waste generated in the first place.
steps: Segregate waste; reduce, reuse, recycle non-biodegradable materials
Compost biodegradable waste; cut down use of non-biodegradable items (e.g., plastic bags)

question: Which of the following groups contain only biodegradable items? (a) Grass, flowers and leather (b) Grass, wood and plastic (c) Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice (d) Cake, wood and grass
solution:
Grass, flowers, leather, wood, fruit-peels, cake, and lime-juice are all natural/organic materials that can be broken down by microorganisms — they are biodegradable. Plastic is non-biodegradable.
So groups (a), (c) and (d) contain only biodegradable items; group (b) is not fully biodegradable because it contains plastic.
steps: Biodegradable = natural/organic, broken down by microbes (grass, flowers, leather, wood, fruit-peels, cake, lime-juice)
Plastic is non-biodegradable
(a), (c), (d) contain only biodegradable items; (b) contains plastic, so it doesn't

question: Which of the following constitute a food-chain? (a) Grass, wheat and mango (b) Grass, goat and human (c) Goat, cow and elephant (d) Grass, fish and goat
solution:
A food chain needs a feeding relationship where each organism is eaten by the next. (a) Grass, wheat, and mango are all producers — no feeding relationship among them. (c) Goat, cow and elephant are all herbivores that don't feed on each other. (d) Fish does not eat grass, and goat does not eat fish — no valid feeding sequence. (b) Grass (producer) is eaten by the goat (herbivore/primary consumer), which is eaten by the human (consumer) — this is a valid feeding sequence.
Correct option: (b) Grass, goat and human.
steps: Food chain needs each organism to be eaten by the next
(a) and (c): all producers or all herbivores — no feeding link
(b) grass→goat→human is a valid feeding chain — answer (b)

question: Which of the following are environment-friendly practices? (a) Carrying cloth-bags to put purchases in while shopping (b) Switching off unnecessary lights and fans (c) Walking to school instead of getting your mother to drop you on her scooter (d) All of the above
solution:
All three practices — using cloth bags (reduces plastic waste), switching off unused electrical appliances (saves energy), and walking instead of using a vehicle (saves fuel, reduces pollution) — are environment-friendly.
Correct option: (d) All of the above.
steps: Cloth bags reduce plastic (non-biodegradable) waste
Switching off lights/fans saves electrical energy
Walking instead of a scooter saves fuel and cuts pollution — answer (d)

question: What will happen if we kill all the organisms in one trophic level?
solution: Killing all organisms in one trophic level would disrupt the flow of energy through the food chain/web. Organisms at the next higher trophic level (which fed on the removed level) would lose their food source and face starvation, decline in number, or be forced to migrate/find alternate food. Meanwhile, the organisms at the trophic level below (that were being eaten/controlled by the removed level) would no longer face that predation pressure and could increase uncontrollably in number, potentially causing further imbalance (e.g., overgrazing, depleting their own food resource). Overall, the ecological balance of that ecosystem would be seriously disturbed, and effects would ripple through other levels via the food web.
steps: Energy flow through that food chain/web is disrupted
Higher trophic level (predators) starve/decline from food loss
Lower trophic level (prey) may increase unchecked — overall ecosystem imbalance

question: Will the impact of removing all the organisms in a trophic level be different for different trophic levels? Can the organisms of any trophic level be removed without causing any damage to the ecosystem?
solution:
Yes, the impact differs depending on which trophic level is removed. Removing the producers (first trophic level) has the most severe/catastrophic impact, since the entire food chain's energy supply originates from them — every other level depends on them, directly or indirectly, so the whole chain would collapse. Removing a higher (consumer) trophic level is generally less catastrophic for the levels below it (though it disturbs population control of levels below and food supply for levels above).
No trophic level can be removed entirely without causing some damage to the ecosystem, since all levels are interconnected and interdependent in the food web; however, the severity of the damage is not the same for every level — removing lower/foundational levels tends to cause more widespread, severe disruption than removing higher levels.
steps: Removing producers is most catastrophic — whole chain depends on them
Removing higher (consumer) levels disturbs the system but is generally less catastrophic overall
No trophic level can be removed without causing some ecosystem damage, though severity differs

question: What is biological magnification? Will the levels of this magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
solution:
Biological magnification is the phenomenon in which harmful, non-biodegradable chemicals (such as pesticides) that enter an ecosystem get progressively concentrated in the bodies of organisms as they move up successive trophic levels of a food chain, because these substances are not broken down or excreted and instead accumulate in the tissues of organisms.
Yes, the levels of magnification differ across trophic levels — the concentration is lowest in producers and increases at each successive trophic level, becoming highest in organisms at the top of the food chain (e.g., large carnivores, or humans), since they consume large amounts of already-contaminated biomass from lower levels to sustain themselves.
steps: Biological magnification = harmful chemicals accumulate more at each higher trophic level
Chemicals are non-degradable, so they build up in organisms' bodies over time
Concentration is lowest in producers, highest at the top of the food chain — levels differ by trophic level

question: What are the problems caused by the non-biodegradable wastes that we generate?
solution: Non-biodegradable wastes (like plastics, glass, certain chemicals) persist in the environment for very long periods since they cannot be broken down by natural biological processes. This causes: accumulation and pollution of soil, water bodies, and landfills; blocking of drains and sewage systems; harm to animals that ingest or get entangled in such waste (e.g., plastic bags/bottles); and, if toxic, entry into food chains where they can undergo biological magnification, causing serious health effects in organisms at higher trophic levels, including humans.
steps: Persist for very long time, accumulating in soil/water/landfills
Can clog drains, harm/kill wildlife (e.g., plastics)
Toxic ones enter food chains and biomagnify, harming higher trophic levels/humans

question: If all the waste we generate is biodegradable, will this have no impact on the environment?
solution: No, even fully biodegradable waste can still impact the environment. If generated in very large quantities, it takes time to decompose, and while decomposing it can cause temporary but significant problems: foul smell, unsightly accumulation, and breeding grounds for disease-causing organisms and pests; decomposition (especially anaerobic decomposition in landfills or water bodies) can also release gases like methane (a greenhouse gas) and pollute water bodies (e.g., causing eutrophication) if not managed and disposed of properly. So biodegradable waste is not impact-free — proper management/disposal is still necessary.
steps: Large amounts of biodegradable waste still take time to decompose
Can cause bad odour, disease-spread, water pollution before/during decomposition
Decomposition can release gases like methane — impact isn't zero, needs proper management

question: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? What steps are being taken to limit this damage?
solution:
The ozone layer in the upper atmosphere shields the earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. Damage/depletion of this layer allows more UV radiation to reach the earth's surface, which can cause serious harm to living organisms — for example, skin cancer and eye damage in humans, and harm to other organisms and ecosystems — making it a serious environmental concern.
Steps taken to limit the damage: the use of ozone-depleting synthetic chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs, used in refrigerants and fire extinguishers) has been targeted through international agreements — in 1987 the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) secured an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and it is now mandatory for manufacturers worldwide to produce CFC-free refrigerators and similar appliances.
steps: Ozone layer blocks harmful UV radiation from the sun
Its depletion lets more UV reach earth — causes skin cancer, other organism damage
UNEP-led international agreement (1987) froze/curbed CFC production; CFC-free appliances now mandatory
